is a criterion, good many people
are uncertain about the pronuncia-
tion. Is it "ISS-o-late" or "EYE-
so-late"? they ask.


Some dictionaries show both pro-
nunciations. A few list "ISS-o-late"
as first choice. Others give pref-
erence to "EYE-so-late." Which
then is the better pronunciation?


That question can best be an-
swered by repeating the recon-
mendation I have made many times:
When two or more pronunciations
are sanctioned by dictionary con-
sensus, always use the pronuncia-
tion that is used by the people as
a whole, whether it is listed as first
choice or not.


Our choice, therefore, is easy to
make, for "EYE-so-late" strongly prevails in Standard American. In
fact, the "iss" pronunciation is
hardly ever heard in the derivatives
isolation and isolationist ("EYE-so-
late'" or "EYE-so-late'-shun; EYE-so-late'-shun-
ist).


The word photogenic in popular
usage means "especially well suited
as subject for photography." For
example, if your pictures always
flatter you, you are photogenic. If
you are one of those persons who
exclaim, "Please don't take my pic-
ture. I always look like a gargoyle!"
then, unfortunately, you are not
photogenic, and there is no future
for you at all in Hollywood or as
a model.


At any rate, pronounce the word
thus: FOE-toe-JENik (not "Jee-
nik").


The word patio, "a court or open
space within a house," is often heard
as "PAT-ee-oh," which, to me at
least, has an Irish sound. Patio is
Spanish. In that language it has
two syllables only, thus PAHT-yoh.
In America, patios are almost always
found in houses of Spanish or Spain-
influenced architecture. There-
fore, it seems fitting that the word
should retain some of its Spanish
flavor.


In best American usage the word
is pronounced: PAH-tee-oh.


When you use the phrases "have got"
or "have gotten," be sure you are using them.

is the buyers strike" caused by the
hiking of prices for food and drinks.

limited expense accounts.

its monthly report, showed drop
of 27.4 in the consumption of liquor
in Washington in January as con-
pared with the same period last
year. Based on tax collections 353,-
936 gallons were sold here in jan
uary as against 487,550 as in jan
uary, 1916.

apparent consumption of liquor in
the United States for January was
14,S71.157 gallons, which was 20 per
cent below January, 1916.

The promotions, made on recommendation of Inspector Floyd A. Truscott, chief of detectives, carry no increase in pay.

With the promotions, all ten squads in the detective bureau now are headed by officers with the rank of lieutenant or above.

The boned-out breast from half a
2O-pound bird will weigh two to three
pounds and serve three portions.
Make dressing by combining one
cup toasted bread cubes, two table
spoons melted fortified margarine or
butter, three tablespoons hot water,
one-half cup of peeled and diced
orange, one-half cup cubed apples and
one-fourth cup raisins. Season meaty
side of breast with one teaspoon salt
and dash of pepper. Spread meat
with dressing, roll and fasten with
skewers. Place on rack in open pan,
brush breast with melted fat and
bake in slow oven (325'F.) for about
three hours. During the baking, brush
occasionally with melted fat to keep
the meat moist.


Roast a Halt Bird


HALF 20-pound turkey yields more
meat than a 12-pound bird roasted
whole. Clean the half bird in the usual
way and rub the cut side with salt, al
lowing e-eighth teaspoon per pound.
Skewer skin to breast meat on keel
bone edge to prevent shrinking of skin
and to protect the breast meat. Tie
leg just above knuckle joint, securing
it to the tail. Place turkey cut side
down on rack in shallow pan. Brush
with melted fat and cover with fat
moistened cloth. Roast in preheated
oven at 325'F.. allowing Is to 80
minutes per pound.


Make the stufing of your choice,
allowing scant three-fourths cup per
pound of bird as purchased. Mound
dressing on well-greased double thick
ness of waxed paper to approximate
shape of turkey cavity. When bird is
half done. remove from oven and
place paper with dressing on rack.
Replace half turkey. over dressing,
cut side down, and continue roasting
until tender. Spoon fat from pan bot
tom to remoisten cloth. Near the end
of the roasting period, remove cloth
if more browning is desired.

This may be seen in the strife and discord which is kept going by communist Russian agents in general in both the Eastern and Western spheres. If reports in the press are correct, they are making good use of Hitler's three weapons: intimidation, misrepresentation, and divide and conquer.

It has been said that a small boy with a hammer can undo everything that a good workman does. And so we see the United States playing the role of the Good Samaritan to the troubled and needy peoples of the world, who are kept harassed and distressed by the evil influence of communism and its agents. The backers of this destructive creed should know that their evil deeds will sooner or later return on their own heads—with interest added. When Mussolini was overrunning the helpless Ethiopians in Africa, an elderly acquaintance remarked, "The Lord don't love ugly ways!" Mussolini's horrible fate is doubtless still fresh in the memory of mankind.

The Prophet Isaiah cries out, "Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?"

The Watchman said: "The morning cometh, and also the night; if we will inquire, we return cope."

Our risen Lord tells us through His beloved John: Behold, I come quickly; and My reward with Me, to give every man according as his work shall be.

Mullaney was called to the stand at the request of Rep. Anita Garrick, author of the bill, and proved an unfortunate witness for the proponents of the measure. He started by reading a copy of a letter which he said he had written to a number of outside corporations doing business in Alaska and from which taxes were due and collectible.

The letter pointed out that all corporations doing business in Alaska are required by law to keep their books and records in Alaska for the examination of the Tax Commissioner. It then went on to say that he, Mullaney, would be willing to undertake a trip to Seattle for the purpose of examining the books, if this would be satisfactory to the companies. Replies read by Mullaney indicated that this would be very satisfactory, and that the companies appreciated the saving they would make if they were not required to present their records in the Territory.

Why Make Trips? These letters started a round of discussion, during which Maurice Johnson asked: "Do you mean you want to have men go outside, at Territorial expense, to examine books which are required to be kept in Alaska?"

Mullaney hedged slightly and explained that in some instances the companies do business both in and out of the Territory, and that it would be unreasonable, and perhaps impossible, to require them to have all of their records in Alaska.

of all literate citizens in the pro-
cesses of policy decision and govern-
ment." It was further stated that
the dominant Democratic organiza-
tion has not been responsive to the
will of the people," and that evidence
of its "mistrust of the people is
found in the constitution as well as
statutory acts.

was defeated by Senator Byrd in
the Democratic primaries last
August, the new organization is in-
tended to function as an independ-
ent, non-fractional body, with em-
phasis on principles rather than on
individuals or cliques.

phlet urged abolition of the poll tax,
election of more major State off-
icials by popular vote, "a definite
source of revenue" earmarked for
education purposes, revision of the
tax laws, further development of
the seafood industry, an industrial
policy recognizing "the just and
equal rights of both management
and labor," judicial reforms and
studies aimed at State government
economies by reduction of the num-
ber of employees.

up entirely of Democrats, Mr.
Hutchinson emphasized in announc-
ing its formation that it was inde-

national organization. He said the
group does not plan to start a "third
party movement" and the commit-
tee had no intention of offering a
slate of candidates for this year's
General Assembly elections or other
public offices.

into the Democratic Party," Mr.
Hutchinson emphasized. "This is
not put forward in the interest of
any one individual but in the in-
terest of all the people of Virginia."

The commissioners today received a report—more than 100 pages long—on the corporation counsel's investigation of Capt. Joseph W. Conroy's charge that Chief Clement Murphy has contributed nothing but "demoralization" to the Fire Department.

The city heads will not make the report public at present. A spokesman said that whether the report ever is made public depends on the way this thing develops from here on.

A copy of the document, one of the most exhaustive ever prepared by the municipal law department, will be sent to Chief Murphy's lawyer, Martin F. O'Donoghue, as soon as the Commissioners have had a chance to study the findings.

Chief Murphy and Mr. O'Donoghue then presumably will be given their first chance to answer the charges.

Another person who doubtless will be heard from before the Commissioners make up their minds about the long-simmering controversy is Daniel B. Maher, newly appointed special assistant corporation counsel in charge of investigations. Mr. Maher will move into the District Building Monday.

Charge Made Before House Unit.

Oliver Gasch, Milton D. Norman and John J. Donnelly, Jr., assistants in the office of the corporation counsel, prepared the report after investigating Capt. Conroy's charge, made last June before House District subcommittee.

Capt. Conroy, president of the Firemen's Association, Local 36, was summoned before the Commissioners shortly after that hearing to detail his charges and supply the names of witnesses, who, he said, would bear out his statements.

The city heads then turned this material over to their legal experts and asked them to investigate it. They indicated they would prefer charges against Chief Murphy if the assertions were borne out by evidence—or against Capt. Conroy if they were not.

Although the corporation counsel's procedure since then has been so secret that even Commissioner John Russell Young said yesterday he did not know what was in the report, hints as to its contents have been leaking out for weeks.

Report Believed Highly Critical

The hints add up to these conclusions:

1. That the report is highly critical of Chief Murphy's administration, and in general supports Capt. Conroy's charge of demoralization.
2. That the report is based on an admittedly one-sided investigation at which witnesses have been those who presumably would support Capt. Conroy.
